CRED app and the Synth framework

An Indian credit-card payments app that moved its whole product to a dark neumorphic interface and open-sourced the framework in 2021.

Source
CRED-CLUB/synth-android on GitHub (archived copy)
Creator
CRED (Dreamplug Technologies)
Made
2020–2021 (adopted after late 2019; Synth open-sourced 18 January 2021)
Style
Neumorphism (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Tactile, premium, quiet
Evidence
Inspected the Synth README banner (2560 × 1280, hosted on i.imgur.com), which shows CRED app screens on phones. The blog post was read from its Wayback capture of 26 January 2021; the live URL now redirects to the CRED home page. The app itself and the blog’s video were not inspected.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

CRED’s blog post “World, meet Synth: Open-sourcing our Neumorphic UI framework” (18 January 2021) says the style “piqued the interest of a few of our designers”, who mocked it up “as a side project”, and that the company then decided “to not just have a few screens but the entire product adopt the Neumorphic aesthetic”.

It adds: “we had to optimize for lights, shadows, gradients, and more in our framework.” Synth was released for Android and iOS under the Apache 2.0 License; the Android repository was created on 12 January 2021.

The Synth README says the library “works over base color concept and derives light and dark colors from base color itself”.

Observed

  • Three phones rendered as dark charcoal slabs on a charcoal background, tilted diagonally.
  • Pill buttons (“Add new”, “View details”) and header chips rise from the dark surface with soft dark shadows and faint light edges. A “Pay more” button is filled blue.
  • Credit-card images and notification cards are in saturated colors (green, mustard, purple, terracotta), which break the single-surface rule.
  • Text is a light, lowercase geometric sans-serif in pale gray; the “synth by CRED” logotype is a copper gradient.

Why it belongs

The strongest evidence found that the style reached a large production app, and it shows the dark variant that most concepts skip. The colored cards are content (the user’s credit cards); the chrome around them keeps to one surface.

Borrow

Derive the light and dark shadow colors from one base color, as Synth does, so a theme change keeps the relief consistent.

What to review next

  • Capture current CRED app screens or the Synth sample app to check whether the app still uses the style.
